Victory in Christ
vĭk´tō-ry ĭn krīst
n. phrase (the believer's conquest over sin, death and the world, possessed by union with the One who won it)
Greek nikos, victory, and nikao, to conquer — the root of the name Nicodemus and of the seven promises to him that overcometh in Revelation. The New Testament's victory is always spoken of as given, shared or already won.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Victory in Christ is a gift with a giver named: “thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (1Co 15:57). Its instrument is faith: “this is the victory that overcometh the world, even our faith” (1Jn 5:4). Its measure exceeds survival: “in all these things we are more than conquerors through him that loved us” (Rom 8:37). It is a procession the believer is led in: “thanks be unto God, which always causeth us to triumph in Christ” (2Co 2:14). And it was won in public at the cross: “having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it” (Col 2:15).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines victory as conquest; the defeat of an enemy in battle, or of an antagonist in contest; a gaining of the superiority in war or combat; and, figuratively, the advantage or superiority gained over spiritual enemies, over passions and appetites, or over temptations.

VICTORY, n. Conquest; the defeat of an enemy in battle, or of an antagonist in contest; a gaining of the superiority in war or combat.

2. The advantage or superiority gained over spiritual enemies, over passions and appetites, or over temptations, or in any struggle or competition.

Thanks be to God, who giveth us the victory, through our Lord Jesus Christ. 1 Cor. 15.

Key Scripture

1Co 15:57 — "But thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ."

1Jn 5:4 — "For whatsoever is born of God overcometh the world: and this is the victory that overcometh the world, even our faith."

Rom 8:37 — "Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him that loved us."

2Co 2:14 — "Now thanks be unto God, which always causeth us to triumph in Christ, and maketh manifest the savour of his knowledge by us in every place."

Col 2:15 — "And having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it."

Modern Corruption

Victory is preached as a state the believer achieves, and every text has it given, shared, or already won by someone else.

expand to see more

The grammar of these verses is the doctrine. God giveth us the victory. We are conquerors through him that loved us. God causeth us to triumph. Christ spoiled the powers and triumphed over them in it — in the cross, before any believer had fought anything. The victorious-life teaching that flourished in the last two centuries reversed the grammar, making victory a plateau a Christian reaches by surrender or technique, and it left a trail of people who had been told they should be living above sin and could not honestly say they were. Romans 7 is in the Bible so that they would not be surprised.

Romans 8:37 is the strongest of these and its context is a list of what has not been removed: tribulation, distress, persecution, famine, nakedness, peril, sword — in all these things we are more than conquerors. Not after them, not by escaping them. The conquest is not the absence of the enemies but the certainty that none of them can separate from the love of God, and the following verses pile up everything that might try. That is a victory compatible with dying, which is the only kind the martyrs had.

Second Corinthians 2:14 has a detail the English hides. God causeth us to triumph in Christ — the verb pictures a Roman triumph, the victorious general's procession through the city, and Paul's place in it is not obvious. The captives walked in those processions too, and the incense that was sweet to the crowd was the smell of death to the condemned. Paul says exactly that in the next verses: we are unto God a sweet savour of Christ, to the one the savour of death unto death, to the other of life unto life. The believer's part in the victory is to be led in it, and the leading is Christ's.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek nikos (G3534), victory; nikao (G3528), to overcome, conquer; hupernikao (G5245), to more than conquer; thriambeuo (G2358), to lead in triumph.

expand to see more

Greek nikos (G3534) — victory; 1 Corinthians 15:54–57, Matthew 12:20, 1 John 5:4.

Greek hupernikomen (G5245) — we are more than conquerors; Romans 8:37 only.

Greek thriambeuo (G2358) — to lead in triumph; 2 Corinthians 2:14, Colossians 2:15 — both occurrences.

Usage

"“Which giveth us the victory” — the grammar is the doctrine."

"“In all these things we are more than conquerors” — in them, not after them."

"“Triumphing over them in it” — in the cross, before anyone had fought."
